title: When is a better LLM worth paying for? Stochastic Optimization with Switching Mixed-Fidelity Oracles

paper.title: When is a better LLM worth paying for? Stochastic Optimization with Switching Mixed-Fidelity Oracles
paper.abstract:
Abstract † † ⋄ Tianjiao Li was at MIT when most of this work was performed. Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used upstream of decision-making to clean data, detect label errors, and reconstruct missing values. Yet LLM-assisted data curation creates a new operational tradeoff: higher-fidelity models and richer prompts can be substantially more expensive, while the value of this additional fidelity depends on the downstream optimization accuracy. This raises the central question of this work: when should one pay for a better LLM, given a specific downstream task at hand? We study this question through stochastic optimization with mixed-fidelity first-order oracles, which can have systematic bias and state-dependent variance. We develop two cost-aware algorithmic frameworks that allow adaptive switching between stochastic oracles. With known bias, the first meta-algorithm applies a restarted, cost-aware policy that adaptively selects oracle fidelity across optimization stages. Its cumulative cost is no larger than that of the best fixed oracle in hindsight and can be substantially smaller. With unknown bias, we develop a budgeted certification scheme that uses occasional trusted-gradient evaluations to certify the optimization progress and eliminate unsuccessful oracle sources, and show an explicit tradeoff between certification cost and delayed detection of biased sources.
We provide concrete realizations of these meta-algorithms by applying biased stochastic gradient extrapolation (SGE) and recursive regularization under state-dependent noise as subroutines.
Synthetic and LLM-completion experiments illustrate the qualitative switching behavior predicted by the theory: the adaptive policy skips several expensive LLM oracles and substantially reduces cumulative cost relative to fixed high-fidelity alternatives while achieving comparable accuracy. Our studies demonstrate that, when information quality can be purchased at different prices, the right fidelity need not be fixed; it depends on how valuable additional accuracy is at the current stage of the downstream decision problem.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Large language models (LLMs) are evolving rapidly, with a growing number of models available through commercial APIs and open-source platforms. These models are increasingly used not only to make predictions, but also to prepare the data on which downstream decisions are based . Recent work uses LLMs for data cleaning and matching ( Zhang et al., 2024 ; Parciak et al., 2024 ; Peeters et al., 2025 ) , missing-value imputation ( Hayat and Hasan, 2025 ; He et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025b ) , denoising recommendation data ( Wang et al., 2025c ; Wang et al., 2025a ) , and data annotation ( Gilardi et al., 2023 ; Goel et al., 2023 ; Ye et al., 2025 ) . In these applications, choosing a model or prompt affects not only the cost of obtaining the data, but also its statistical quality for the downstream task. Stronger models, richer prompts, or ensembles may produce more accurate data, but often at a substantially higher price. The key question we consider in this work is: when is additional fidelity worth paying for? We explore this in the context of downstream optimization tasks, like supervised machine learning. Consider a synthetic experiment on the Aspiring Minds hiring dataset with 10% missing covariates (randomly masked). The goal is to predict ComputerProgramming scores of the candidates from numeric independent features like performance in high school, tier of the undergraduate college, agreeableness, etc. We ask different LLM model–prompt pipelines to reconstruct the missing values, which induces a stochastic-gradient oracle for downstream linear regression, with different fidelities. Table 1 reports their cost and representative fidelity parameters. Even within one model family, richer prompting can significantly change downstream fidelity at almost the same cost. Across different models, price and fidelity are not necessarily monotone. For example, Claude Sonnet 5 costs substantially more than Claude Haiku 4.5 while attaining essentially the same downstream objective in this experiment. Conversely, averaging several high-fidelity completions reduces bias but is much more expensive than a simple completion with GPT Nano. Thus neither “always use the cheapest model” nor “always use the best model” is compelling. Table 1: Representative LLM-completion pipelines at 10% missingness. At coarse accuracy scales, a low-cost oracle can be sufficient for continued progress; as optimization approaches x ∗ x^{*} , higher-fidelity oracles become worthwhile or necessary. The actual switching points depend jointly on oracle cost, bias, variance, and the current optimization scale. This question motivates us to propose a progress-dependent optimization strategy. Rather than committing to one oracle throughout optimization, we divide the optimization trajectory into stages of progressively finer accuracy. At a stage with current error scale R R , an oracle does not need to be the most accurate one available; it only needs to be accurate enough to support the next constant-factor reduction in optimization error. Among the oracles that can achieve this reduction, we choose the most cost-efficient one, i.e., the one with the smallest total stage cost. Therefore, when far from the optimum, a cheap but relatively noisy or biased oracle can be the most economical choice. As the target radius shrinks, the required bias level becomes more stringent and residual noise becomes more important, causing the algorithm to switch to higher-fidelity sources. This design is informed by recent studies on state-dependent behavior of stochastic optimization algorithms ( Woodworth and Srebro, 2021 ; Juditsky et al., 2023 ; Ilandarideva et al., 2025 ) . In the classical state-independent setting ( Nemirovski et al., 2009 ; Lan, 2012 ) , the stochastic gradient noise is assumed to be uniformly bounded over the domain, which can be restrictive for important applications such as generalized linear regression with unbounded regressors. Under the more general state-dependent model, the noise level varies with the optimality state: the state-dependent component decreases as the iterates approach the optimum, while the residual component captures the irreducible noise at the optimum. With multiple priced oracles, these different scalings imply that the relative cost-efficiency of the oracles can change across optimization stages; thus there need not be a single oracle that is uniformly optimal throughout the trajectory. In our illustrative experiment with oracles shown in Table 1 , this logic produces the progression from inexpensive Nano pipelines to Luna and eventually an ensemble, while skipping several more expensive alternatives like Sonnet altogether. sections.heading: 1.1 Contributions.
sections.text: Our main contributions lie in the design and analysis of cost-efficient adaptive oracle-switching meta-algorithms, together with concrete stochastic optimization subroutines and LLM experiments. • Multistage oracle-switching with known bias. We develop a generic meta-algorithm that uses a chosen stochastic optimization subroutine across stages, so that the current squared-distance radius is reduced by a constant factor. At each stage, the policy selects the most cost-efficient oracle for achieving the next contraction among all oracles with admissible bias. As one concrete contraction subroutine, we analyze a strongly convex variant of stochastic gradient extrapolation (SGE) ( Lan and Zhou, 2018 ) under state-dependent noise and persistent bias. For unbiased oracles, the cumulative cost of our framework is no larger than that of the best fixed oracle in hindsight, and the savings can be up to Θ ⁡ ( K / log ⁡ K ) \Theta(K/\log K) over K K stages. With biased oracles, the framework can exploit cheaper sources early while ultimately reaching the accuracy scale allowed by lower-bias sources. • Characterizing cost with respect to desired accuracy: The stagewise formulation yields explicit operational criteria for comparing oracle cost and fidelity. We characterize when one oracle is dominated by another and derive stage-dependent break-even prices that quantify how much one should be willing to pay for a higher-fidelity source at a given downstream accuracy level. Our results can help vendors check a simple condition dependent on their downstream task, and decide which oracles are useful in their pipeline. • Budgeted certification with unknown bias. When bias parameters are unavailable or hard-to-estimate, we develop a second meta-algorithm based on occasional trusted projected-gradient certification. We introduce a budget parameter to control how much uncertified training can be performed before the next checkpoint; failed sources are removed permanently while any certifiable progress is retained. We further show that recursive regularization combined with biased SGE provides a concrete projected-gradient reduction subroutine for certification, and characterize the resulting tradeoff between frequent certification and delayed detection of biased sources. • Empirical validation. We conducted controlled simulations and LLM-completion experiments on the Aspiring Minds hiring dataset. The adaptive strategy exhibits the predicted stage-dependent switching and achieves substantial cost savings relative to strategies with a fixed stochastic oracle. At 10% missingness, for example, the adaptive policy follows Nano LR-short-7 (SO2) ⟶ Nano LR-10 (SO4) ⟶ Luna (SO5) ⟶ Avg. Haiku+Sonnet (SO8) , \displaystyle\text{Nano LR-short-7 (SO2)}\longrightarrow\text{Nano LR-10 (SO4)}\longrightarrow\text{Luna (SO5)}\longrightarrow\text{Avg. Haiku+Sonnet (SO8)}, skipping several more expensive alternatives. The cumulative cost is about $72, versus about $240 for always using the best oracle, a reduction of roughly 70% while reaching the same accuracy scale. Our experiments also provide clear evidence for the certification frequency tradeoff when the bias parameters are unknown.

sections.heading: LLM data curation and noisy supervision.
sections.text: LLMs are increasingly used to improve data quality before it enters a downstream learning or decision problem. For missing-data imputation, Hayat and Hasan (2025) use contextual information from pre-trained language models, He et al. (2025) combine graph-augmented prompting with an ensemble of LLMs, and Wang et al. (2025b) develop an LLM-based spatiotemporal imputation model for highly sparse remote-sensing data. Related work uses LLMs for general-purpose data cleaning and matching ( Zhang et al., 2024 ; Parciak et al., 2024 ; Peeters et al., 2025 ) , and for identifying or correcting noisy interactions in recommender systems ( Wang et al., 2025c ; Wang et al., 2025a ) . On the labeling side, LLMs can serve as scalable annotators or assist human annotators ( Gilardi et al., 2023 ; Goel et al., 2023 ) ; recent work also studies how to detect label errors ( Nahum et al., 2025 ) and train classifiers robustly from LLM-generated noisy labels ( Ye et al., 2025 ) . These papers primarily ask how LLMs can improve upstream data quality. Our focus is complementary: given several data-generation or curation pipelines with different costs and fidelities, we ask how their value changes with the stage of the downstream optimization problem.

sections.heading: Cost-aware model selection and data markets.
sections.text: Closest to our cost perspective are systems that choose different models for different inference queries. Chen et al. (2024) propose FrugalGPT which exploits heterogeneous model prices and task performance to construct lower-cost cascades. Ong et al. (2025) propose RouteLLM that learns to route prompts between stronger and weaker models using preference data. In a concurrent work, Belloni et al. (2026) develop an online learning approach to adaptively query and select LLM APIs. Our setting is different: the source is selected according to the progress of a downstream optimization algorithm , rather than independently for each inference query. More broadly, the economics literature studies data as a priced asset and analyzes data markets, valuation, and pricing distortions ( Acemoglu et al., 2022 ; Farboodi and Veldkamp, 2023 ) . The value of clean versus corrupted data also appears outside the LLM setting. Denoising is central to diffusion-based generative modeling ( Ho et al., 2020 ) , while Daras et al. (2025) explicitly quantify how noisy training samples trade off against clean samples in ambient diffusion.

sections.heading: Stochastic, multi-fidelity, and multilevel optimization.
sections.text: Multi-fidelity optimization and simulation exploit sources of different costs and accuracies, often to reduce the number of expensive evaluations ( Peherstorfer et al., 2018 ; Kandasamy et al., 2017 ) . In first-order methods and stochastic approximation ( Polyak, 1990 ; Nemirovski et al., 2009 ) , inexact-oracle models quantify the effect of deterministic errors ( Devolder et al., 2014 ) , while biased stochastic-gradient analyses study persistent gradient bias; see, e.g., Ajalloeian and Stich (2020) . Our noise model is also related to stochastic optimization with state-dependent noise conditions that replace a uniform variance bound by one that decreases near the solution ( Gower et al., 2019 ; Aybat et al., 2019 ; Gower et al., 2021 ; Woodworth and Srebro, 2021 ; Kotsalis et al., 2022 ; Juditsky et al., 2023 ; Ilandarideva et al., 2025 ; Rodomanov et al., 2024 ) . As one concrete implementation of our meta-algorithms, we use SGE-type acceleration proposed by Lan and Zhou (2018) , whose extrapolation structure is well suited to state-dependent noise as shown in Ilandarideva et al. (2025) . Moreover, our unknown-bias construction is related to learning from weak or inexpensive information augmented by a small trusted source ( Ratner et al., 2017 ; Hendrycks et al., 2018 ; Angelopoulos et al., 2023 ) , and uses recursive regularization for gradient minimization in stochastic settings ( Allen-Zhu, 2018 ; Foster et al., 2019 ) for certification. Closely related to our bias–variance–cost perspective is the multilevel Monte Carlo (MLMC) line of work on stochastic optimization with biased oracles. Hu et al. (2021) ; Hu et al. (2024) study a hierarchy of increasingly accurate and increasingly expensive biased stochastic oracles and design MLMC gradient estimators that exploit the joint tradeoff among bias, variance, and query cost. This line builds on MLMC and randomized-debiasing ideas for stochastic approximation ( Giles, 2008 ; Blanchet and Glynn, 2015 ; Dereich and Müller-Gronbach, 2019 ; Blanchet et al., 2017 ; Beatson and Adams, 2019 ; Asi et al., 2021 ) . In particular, Beatson and Adams (2019) tune randomized telescoping estimators according to optimization progress per unit of computation, while Asi et al. (2021) use multilevel randomization to construct low-bias, low-cost estimators for optimization subroutines. Our setting shares the principle that lower bias should be purchased only when it is worth the additional cost, but the oracle model and algorithmic mechanism are different. The MLMC framework assumes a structured approximation hierarchy and exploits coupled difference estimators across adjacent fidelity levels. By contrast, we allow a finite collection of heterogeneous black-box stochastic oracles that need not be nested, ordered by fidelity, or coupled through difference estimators.

sections.heading: 2 Applications: LLM-generated labels and completed data
sections.text: In this section, we provide two concrete examples showing how the mixed-fidelity assumptions arise in LLM-assisted data pipelines. The first considers LLM-generated or LLM-corrected labels; while the second considers LLM reconstruction of missing covariates. In both cases, stronger models, richer prompts, ensembles, or human review can be represented as more expensive oracles with different bias and variance parameters.

sections.heading: 3 Known bias: cost-aware oracle-switching
sections.text: In this section, we introduce a multistage adaptive oracle switching strategy assuming the bias parameters { ℬ λ } λ = 1 ℓ \{\mathcal{B}_{\lambda}\}_{\lambda=1}^{\ell} are known. To enable the design of the multistage meta-algorithm, we first assume access to a stochastic optimization subroutine that can reduce the current expected squared distance to the optimum by a constant factor at a predictable cost. A concrete choice of an efficient subroutine will be discussed in Subsection 3.1 . Definition 1 (Distance-contraction subroutine) . Consider an optimization subroutine 𝖢𝗈𝗇𝗍𝗋𝖺𝖼𝗍 ⁡ ( y , R , SO λ ) , \mathsf{Contract}(y,R;\mathrm{SO}_{\lambda}), which takes an initial point y y , a target radius R R , and a stochastic oracle SO λ \mathrm{SO}_{\lambda} as inputs. Associated with the subroutine are a bias-admissibility condition 𝖠𝖽𝗆 C ​ ( R , ℬ λ ) \mathsf{Adm}_{\rm C}(R,\mathcal{B}_{\lambda}) and an oracle complexity bound T ⁡ ( R , λ ) T(R,\lambda) . We say that 𝖢𝗈𝗇𝗍𝗋𝖺𝖼𝗍 \mathsf{Contract} is a valid distance-contraction subroutine if, whenever 𝔼 ​ ‖ y − x ∗ ‖ 2 ≤ R 2 and 𝖠𝖽𝗆 C ​ ( R , ℬ λ ) ​ holds , \mathbb{E}\|y-x^{*}\|^{2}\leq R^{2}\quad\text{and}\quad\mathsf{Adm}_{\rm C}(R,\mathcal{B}_{\lambda})\text{ holds}, it uses at most T ⁡ ( R , λ ) T(R,\lambda) calls to SO λ \mathrm{SO}_{\lambda} and returns y + y^{+} satisfying 𝔼 ​ ‖ y + − x ∗ ‖ 2 ≤ R 2 2 . \mathbb{E}\|y^{+}-x^{*}\|^{2}\leq\frac{R^{2}}{2}. Here 𝖠𝖽𝗆 C ​ ( R , ℬ λ ) \mathsf{Adm}_{\rm C}(R,\mathcal{B}_{\lambda}) represents the bias requirement needed for the stochastic oracle SO λ to achieve the desired contraction, which depends on oracle SO λ only through its bias level ℬ λ \mathcal{B}_{\lambda} . In contrast, the complexity bound T ⁡ ( R , λ ) T(R,\lambda) depends on problem parameters such as L L and μ \mu , and other oracle characteristics such as its variance parameters σ λ , ∗ 2 \sigma_{\lambda,*}^{2} and ℒ λ \mathcal{L}_{\lambda} . The initial point y y in Definition 1 may itself be random. The expectation is taken over both the randomness of y y and the fresh randomness used by the subroutine. Algorithm 1 requires only this input–output guarantee as in Definition 1 , so the inner subroutine may be the classic stochastic approximation type methods, variance-reduced methods, or any other procedure with a known bias-admissibility condition and sample complexity budget. In particular, at stage s s , given 𝔼 ​ ‖ y s − 1 − x ∗ ‖ 2 ≤ R s − 1 2 , \mathbb{E}\|y^{s-1}-x^{*}\|^{2}\leq R_{s-1}^{2}, the algorithm selects, among the admissible oracles, the one with the lowest cost for producing the next contraction. (2024) . Therefore, our paper focuses on the more challenging unknown bias setting. Therefore, in this section, we assume occasional access to an expensive certification module 𝒞 \mathcal{C} that returns the trusted gradient ∇ f ​ ( y ) \nabla f(y) at a cost c cert > 0 c_{\rm cert}>0 per query. The module is accurate enough to certify optimization progress, but can be too expensive to use for routine training. This setup follows the broad principle of combining abundant machine-generated information with a small amount of trusted data; see, e.g., Hendrycks et al. (2018) ; Angelopoulos et al. (2023) . The price of the certification module c cert c_{\rm cert} introduces an additional operational decision: How often should the optimization progress be certified? Certifying after every stage of contraction detects overly biased sources quickly, but repeatedly pays for the expensive trusted information. Certifying too rarely saves trusted queries but can spend substantial training cost on an oracle that has already become too biased to achieve the desired accuracy. Our meta-algorithm proposed in this section interpolates between these extremes using a specified budget B B on uncertified training expenditure. Remark 2 . We analyze exact trusted-gradient certification in order to isolate this certification-frequency tradeoff from the statistical problem of constructing the certificate itself. In applications, the certification module 𝒞 \mathcal{C} may instead be constructed using a sufficiently large trusted sample, expert-reviewed observations, or repeated measurements. Standard concentration arguments can then construct a high-probability confidence bound for the projected-gradient norm. We leave the joint tradeoff among trusted-sample size, statistical precision, and certification frequency for a stochastic certification oracle to future work. sections.heading: 6 Numerical experiments
sections.text: In this section, we use simulated and LLM-based experiments to illustrate three key implications of our framework: (i) the cost-minimizing oracle can change with the optimization scale, (ii) stage-dependent switching can be substantially cheaper than committing to a single oracle, and (iii) when oracle biases are unknown, there is a clean tradeoff between frequent certification and delayed detection of biased sources.

sections.text: We first corroborate the switching mechanism in a strongly convex linear-regression problem with two unbiased stochastic oracles. At coarse accuracy, Algorithm 1 selects SO1 because its lower price more than offsets its larger variance. sections.text: For completed dataset λ \lambda , a sampled-row gradient is 𝒢 λ ​ ( x , j ) = θ ~ λ , j ​ ( θ ~ λ , j ⊤ ​ x − y j ) . \mathcal{G}_{\lambda}(x;j)=\widetilde{\theta}_{\lambda,j}(\widetilde{\theta}_{\lambda,j}^{\top}x-y_{j}). For ensemble oracles, we average component gradients on the same sampled row and sum their component costs. To compare optimization trajectories on a common scale, we divide the one-time full-dataset completion price by the number of rows to obtain an equivalent per-observation query price; a mini-batch of size m m is charged m m times this price. This is only an accounting device for comparing information costs. Our goal in this experiment is to place heterogeneous information sources on a common cost scale, rather than to reproduce the billing mechanics of a particular deployment. The completion pipelines incur an upfront cost for producing datasets of different fidelities, whereas the optimization framework is expressed in terms of oracle-query costs. We therefore amortize each completion cost across observations and use the resulting per-row price to compare the information consumed along different optimization trajectories. Lastly, we would like to comment that the regression experiments in Subsections 6.2 – 6.3 are intentionally chosen as a controlled setting in which the clean downstream objective and the mixed-fidelity oracle parameters can be measured directly. Our purpose is not to claim that regression exhausts LLM-assisted decision pipelines, but to test the mechanism predicted by the theory while holding the downstream optimization problem fixed. The same framework applies whenever alternative data-generation procedures induce stochastic first-order information of different cost and fidelity, including downstream estimation, prediction-and-optimization, and decision-support pipelines.

sections.heading: 7 Concluding remarks
sections.text: The central message is that the optimal use of mixed-fidelity information depends critically on the stage of downstream optimization. A cheap source can be the economically correct choice when the optimizer is far from the solution, even if its fidelity would be unacceptable at the final accuracy. Conversely, high fidelity is worth paying for only when it enables a more cost-efficient algorithmic progress or a lower attainable bias floor. The resulting break-even prices connect the optimization analysis to classical ideas on the value of information: information should be purchased according to its decision value, not its intrinsic accuracy alone ( Howard, 1966 ; Sims, 2003 ) . This perspective also suggests a complementary way to benchmark LLMs. General evaluation efforts such as HELM and Chatbot Arena provide valuable standardized comparisons of model capabilities and human preferences; see, e.g., Bommasani et al. (2023) ; Chiang et al. (2024) . For optimization-driven applications, however, a single global rank may not identify the economically best model. A useful task-specific “oracle card” could report not only benchmark accuracy and token price, but also downstream quantities such as bias, residual variance, and state-dependent variance on a representative calibration set. For data labeling, these quantities can be estimated using repeated or trusted labels; for data completion, they can be estimated from a held-out fully observed subset. Such reporting would make it possible to translate model improvements directly into stage-dependent willingness-to-pay curves such as ( 4.3 ). Although LLM-assisted data curation motivates this work, the framework is broader. The same mixed-fidelity structure arises when stochastic first-order information is produced by human experts of different skill levels, crowd workers, sensors of different precision, approximate simulators, laboratory measurements, or computational solvers with different tolerances. Interesting future directions include learning oracle parameters online rather than from calibration data and allowing correlated errors across different data sources. Our analysis can be used in general for any portfolio of stochastic oracles. For LLM-based oracles, we abstract away several deployment-specific features. In particular, oracle acquisition may involve fixed setup costs in addition to marginal query costs; trusted certification may itself be estimated from finite samples; and practical implementations may estimate fidelity parameters only approximately. The empirical cost normalization and admissibility rules used in Section 6 are intended to expose the stage-dependent switching mechanism rather than to model every feature of a particular API deployment. Extending the framework to jointly learn oracle quality, acquisition cost, and certification uncertainty is an interesting direction for future work.

sections.heading: A.1 Proof of Theorem 1

Stochastic Optimization with Switching Mixed-Fidelity Oracles Swati Gupta ⋆ Tianjiao Li †,⋄ MIT Sloan School of Management ⋆ IBM Research † October 15, 2026 Abstract † † ⋄ Tianjiao Li was at MIT when most of this work was performed. Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used upstream of decision-making to clean data, detect label errors, and reconstruct missing values. Yet LLM-assisted data curation creates a new operational tradeoff: higher-fidelity models and richer prompts can be substantially more expensive, while the value of this additional fidelity depends on the downstream optimization accuracy. This raises the central question of this work: when should one pay for a better LLM, given a specific downstream task at hand? We study this question through stochastic optimization with mixed-fidelity first-order oracles, which can have systematic bias and state-dependent variance. We develop two cost-aware algorithmic frameworks that allow adaptive switching between stochastic oracles. With known bias, the first meta-algorithm applies a restarted, cost-aware policy that adaptively selects oracle fidelity across optimization stages. Its cumulative cost is no larger than that of the best fixed oracle in hindsight and can be substantially smaller. With unknown bias, we develop a budgeted certification scheme that uses occasional trusted-gradient evaluations to certify the optimization progress and eliminate unsuccessful oracle sources, and show an explicit tradeoff between certification cost and delayed detection of biased sources. We provide concrete realizations of these meta-algorithms by applying biased stochastic gradient extrapolation (SGE) and recursive regularization under state-dependent noise as subroutines. Synthetic and LLM-completion experiments illustrate the qualitative switching behavior predicted by the theory: the adaptive policy skips several expensive LLM oracles and substantially reduces cumulative cost relative to fixed high-fidelity alternatives while achieving comparable accuracy. Our studies demonstrate that, when information quality can be purchased at different prices, the right fidelity need not be fixed; it depends on how valuable additional accuracy is at the current stage of the downstream decision problem. 1 Introduction Large language models (LLMs) are evolving rapidly, with a growing number of models available through commercial APIs and open-source platforms. These models are increasingly used not only to make predictions, but also to prepare the data on which downstream decisions are based . Recent work uses LLMs for data cleaning and matching ( Zhang et al., 2024 ; Parciak et al., 2024 ; Peeters et al., 2025 ) , missing-value imputation ( Hayat and Hasan, 2025 ; He et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025b ) , denoising recommendation data ( Wang et al., 2025c ; Wang et al., 2025a ) , and data annotation ( Gilardi et al., 2023 ; Goel et al., 2023 ; Ye et al., 2025 ) . In these applications, choosing a model or prompt affects not only the cost of obtaining the data, but also its statistical quality for the downstream task. Stronger models, richer prompts, or ensembles may produce more accurate data, but often at a substantially higher price. The key question we consider in this work is: when is additional fidelity worth paying for? We explore this in the context of downstream optimization tasks, like supervised machine learning. Consider a synthetic experiment on the Aspiring Minds hiring dataset with 10% missing covariates (randomly masked). The goal is to predict ComputerProgramming scores of the candidates from numeric independent features like performance in high school, tier of the undergraduate college, agreeableness, etc. We ask different LLM model–prompt pipelines to reconstruct the missing values, which induces a stochastic-gradient oracle for downstream linear regression, with different fidelities. Table 1 reports their cost and representative fidelity parameters. Even within one model family, richer prompting can significantly change downstream fidelity at almost the same cost. Across different models, price and fidelity are not necessarily monotone. For example, Claude Sonnet 5 costs substantially more than Claude Haiku 4.5 while attaining essentially the same downstream objective in this experiment. Conversely, averaging several high-fidelity completions reduces bias but is much more expensive than a simple completion with GPT Nano. Thus neither “always use the cheapest model” nor “always use the best model” is compelling. Table 1: Representative LLM-completion pipelines at 10% missingness. Cost is the one-time full-dataset completion price; Obj. is the clean downstream regression objective. At coarse accuracy scales, a low-cost oracle can be sufficient for continued progress; as optimization approaches x ∗ x^{*} , higher-fidelity oracles become worthwhile or necessary. The actual switching points depend jointly on oracle cost, bias, variance, and the current optimization scale. This question motivates us to propose a progress-dependent optimization strategy. Rather than committing to one oracle throughout optimization, we divide the optimization trajectory into stages of progressively finer accuracy. At a stage with current error scale R R , an oracle does not need to be the most accurate one available; it only needs to be accurate enough to support the next constant-factor reduction in optimization error. Among the oracles that can achieve this reduction, we choose the most cost-efficient one, i.e., the one with the smallest total stage cost. Therefore, when far from the optimum, a cheap but relatively noisy or biased oracle can be the most economical choice. As the target radius shrinks, the required bias level becomes more stringent and residual noise becomes more important, causing the algorithm to switch to higher-fidelity sources. This design is informed by recent studies on state-dependent behavior of stochastic optimization algorithms ( Woodworth and Srebro, 2021 ; Juditsky et al., 2023 ; Ilandarideva et al., 2025 ) . In the classical state-independent setting ( Nemirovski et al., 2009 ; Lan, 2012 ) , the stochastic gradient noise is assumed to be uniformly bounded over the domain, which can be restrictive for important applications such as generalized linear regression with unbounded regressors. Under the more general state-dependent model, the noise level varies with the optimality state: the state-dependent component decreases as the iterates approach the optimum, while the residual component captures the irreducible noise at the optimum. Our main contributions lie in the design and analysis of cost-efficient adaptive oracle-switching meta-algorithms, together with concrete stochastic optimization subroutines and LLM experiments. • Multistage oracle-switching with known bias. We develop a generic meta-algorithm that uses a chosen stochastic optimization subroutine across stages, so that the current squared-distance radius is reduced by a constant factor. At each stage, the policy selects the most cost-efficient oracle for achieving the next contraction among all oracles with admissible bias. As one concrete contraction subroutine, we analyze a strongly convex variant of stochastic gradient extrapolation (SGE) ( Lan and Zhou, 2018 ) under state-dependent noise and persistent bias. For unbiased oracles, the cumulative cost of our framework is no larger than that of the best fixed oracle in hindsight, and the savings can be up to Θ ⁡ ( K / log ⁡ K ) \Theta(K/\log K) over K K stages. With biased oracles, the framework can exploit cheaper sources early while ultimately reaching the accuracy scale allowed by lower-bias sources. • Characterizing cost with respect to desired accuracy: The stagewise formulation yields explicit operational criteria for comparing oracle cost and fidelity. We characterize when one oracle is dominated by another and derive stage-dependent break-even prices that quantify how much one should be willing to pay for a higher-fidelity source at a given downstream accuracy level. Our results can help vendors check a simple condition dependent on their downstream task, and decide which oracles are useful in their pipeline. • Budgeted certification with unknown bias. When bias parameters are unavailable or hard-to-estimate, we develop a second meta-algorithm based on occasional trusted projected-gradient certification. We introduce a budget parameter to control how much uncertified training can be performed before the next checkpoint; failed sources are removed permanently while any certifiable progress is retained. We further show that recursive regularization combined with biased SGE provides a concrete projected-gradient reduction subroutine for certification, and characterize the resulting tradeoff between frequent certification and delayed detection of biased sources. • Empirical validation. We conducted controlled simulations and LLM-completion experiments on the Aspiring Minds hiring dataset. The adaptive strategy exhibits the predicted stage-dependent switching and achieves substantial cost savings relative to strategies with a fixed stochastic oracle. At 10% missingness, for example, the adaptive policy follows Nano LR-short-7 (SO2) ⟶ Nano LR-10 (SO4) ⟶ Luna (SO5) ⟶ Avg. LLMs are increasingly used to improve data quality before it enters a downstream learning or decision problem. For missing-data imputation, Hayat and Hasan (2025) use contextual information from pre-trained language models, He et al. (2025) combine graph-augmented prompting with an ensemble of LLMs, and Wang et al. (2025b) develop an LLM-based spatiotemporal imputation model for highly sparse remote-sensing data. Related work uses LLMs for general-purpose data cleaning and matching ( Zhang et al., 2024 ; Parciak et al., 2024 ; Peeters et al., 2025 ) , and for identifying or correcting noisy interactions in recommender systems ( Wang et al., 2025c ; Wang et al., 2025a ) . On the labeling side, LLMs can serve as scalable annotators or assist human annotators ( Gilardi et al., 2023 ; Goel et al., 2023 ) ; recent work also studies how to detect label errors ( Nahum et al., 2025 ) and train classifiers robustly from LLM-generated noisy labels ( Ye et al., 2025 ) . These papers primarily ask how LLMs can improve upstream data quality. Our focus is complementary: given several data-generation or curation pipelines with different costs and fidelities, we ask how their value changes with the stage of the downstream optimization problem. Cost-aware model selection and data markets. Closest to our cost perspective are systems that choose different models for different inference queries. Chen et al. (2024) propose FrugalGPT which exploits heterogeneous model prices and task performance to construct lower-cost cascades. Ong et al. (2025) propose RouteLLM that learns to route prompts between stronger and weaker models using preference data. In a concurrent work, Belloni et al. (2026) develop an online learning approach to adaptively query and select LLM APIs. Our setting is different: the source is selected according to the progress of a downstream optimization algorithm , rather than independently for each inference query. More broadly, the economics literature studies data as a priced asset and analyzes data markets, valuation, and pricing distortions ( Acemoglu et al., 2022 ; Farboodi and Veldkamp, 2023 ) . The value of clean versus corrupted data also appears outside the LLM setting. Denoising is central to diffusion-based generative modeling ( Ho et al., 2020 ) , while Daras et al. (2025) explicitly quantify how noisy training samples trade off against clean samples in ambient diffusion. Stochastic, multi-fidelity, and multilevel optimization. Multi-fidelity optimization and simulation exploit sources of different costs and accuracies, often to reduce the number of expensive evaluations ( Peherstorfer et al., 2018 ; Kandasamy et al., 2017 ) . In first-order methods and stochastic approximation ( Polyak, 1990 ; Nemirovski et al., 2009 ) , inexact-oracle models quantify the effect of deterministic errors ( Devolder et al., 2014 ) , while biased stochastic-gradient analyses study persistent gradient bias; see, e.g., Ajalloeian and Stich (2020) . Our noise model is also related to stochastic optimization with state-dependent noise conditions that replace a uniform variance bound by one that decreases near the solution ( Gower et al., 2019 ; Aybat et al., 2019 ; Gower et al., 2021 ; Woodworth and Srebro, 2021 ; Kotsalis et al., 2022 ; Juditsky et al., 2023 ; Ilandarideva et al., 2025 ; Rodomanov et al., 2024 ) . As one concrete implementation of our meta-algorithms, we use SGE-type acceleration proposed by Lan and Zhou (2018) , whose extrapolation structure is well suited to state-dependent noise as shown in Ilandarideva et al. (2025) . Moreover, our unknown-bias construction is related to learning from weak or inexpensive information augmented by a small trusted source ( Ratner et al., 2017 ; Hendrycks et al., 2018 ; Angelopoulos et al., 2023 ) , and uses recursive regularization for gradient minimization in stochastic settings ( Allen-Zhu, 2018 ; Foster et al., 2019 ) for certification. Closely related to our bias–variance–cost perspective is the multilevel Monte Carlo (MLMC) line of work on stochastic optimization with biased oracles. Hu et al. (2021) ; Hu et al. (2024) study a hierarchy of increasingly accurate and increasingly expensive biased stochastic oracles and design MLMC gradient estimators that exploit the joint tradeoff among bias, variance, and query cost. This line builds on MLMC and randomized-debiasing ideas for stochastic approximation ( Giles, 2008 ; Blanchet and Glynn, 2015 ; Dereich and Müller-Gronbach, 2019 ; Blanchet et al., 2017 ; Beatson and Adams, 2019 ; Asi et al., 2021 ) . In particular, Beatson and Adams (2019) tune randomized telescoping estimators according to optimization progress per unit of computation, while Asi et al. (2021) use multilevel randomization to construct low-bias, low-cost estimators for optimization subroutines. Our setting shares the principle that lower bias should be purchased only when it is worth the additional cost, but the oracle model and algorithmic mechanism are different. The MLMC framework assumes a structured approximation hierarchy and exploits coupled difference estimators across adjacent fidelity levels. By contrast, we allow a finite collection of heterogeneous black-box stochastic oracles that need not be nested, ordered by fidelity, or coupled through difference estimators. 1.3 Notation and organization Throughout the paper, we let ∥ ⋅ ∥ \|\cdot\| denote the Euclidean norm for vectors and the spectral norm for matrices, and let ⟨ ⋅ , ⋅ ⟩ \langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle denote the Euclidean inner product.
